analysis.subject: chemistry
analysis.pageCoverage: Page covers gas properties and density, Boyle’s law and Charles and Gay-Lussac’s law, derivation of pV equals nRT and its specific forms pv equals RT and p equals rho RT, and the need for absolute temperature measured in Kelvin and Rankine.

overview.headline: Ideal gas equation links pressure, volume and temperature

keyPoints.point: Students learn that gas properties of pressure, temperature, mass and volume determine the state of a gas
keyPoints.quote: including the gas pressure p, temperature T, mass m, and volume V that contains the gas.

keyPoints.point: Students learn that Boyle’s law states the product of pressure and volume is constant for an ideal gas
keyPoints.quote: The product of pressure and volume is exactly a constant for an ideal gas.

keyPoints.point: Students learn that combined gas laws give the single equation of state pV equals nRT
keyPoints.quote: The gas laws of Boyle and Charles and Gay-Lussac can be combined into a single equation of state given in red at the center of the slide:

keyPoints.point: Students learn that the equation requires absolute temperature that begins at absolute zero in Kelvin or Rankine
keyPoints.quote: Also be aware that the temperature given in the equation of state must be an absolute temperature that begins at absolute zero.

keyTerms.gloss: force per area exerted by gas that changes with volume and temperature
keyTerms.quote: including the gas pressure p, temperature T, mass m, and volume V that contains the gas.

keyTerms.gloss: ratio of mass to volume for a gas sample
keyTerms.quote: This allows us to define a single additional property called the gas density rho (ρ), which is the ratio of mass to volume.

keyTerms.gloss: relationship where pressure and volume product stays constant for ideal gas
keyTerms.quote: This relationship between pressure and volume is called Boyle’s Law in honor of Robert Boyle who first observed it in 1660.

keyTerms.gloss: single combined relation that links gas pressure, volume and temperature
keyTerms.quote: The gas laws of Boyle and Charles and Gay-Lussac can be combined into a single equation of state given in red at the center of the slide:

keyTerms.gloss: temperature scale that starts at absolute zero and is needed for gas law
keyTerms.quote: Also be aware that the temperature given in the equation of state must be an absolute temperature that begins at absolute zero.
